newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's Ahern sees talks with Sinn Fein this week.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Ahern sees talks with Sinn Fein this week.

text.p: Bertie Ahern, expecting to be named Irish Prime Minister aftere a cliffhanger poll, said on Sunday that he expected to hold talks with Sinn Fein this week to sound out chances of a new truce by its IRA allies.
Ahern, leader of the opposition Fianna Fail party, told state RTE radio that he expected to have contact with Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams this week.
"I would say I would have contact with Gerry Adams over the next week if this is possible," Ahern said.

British and Irish government officials have reopened contact with Sinn Fein which they broke in February last year to punish the party for the Irish Republican Army (IRA) decision to end a 17-month truce.

Britain's new Labour government has held two rounds of talks with Sinn Fein and Prime Minister John Bruton's Dublin government also held talks with the party, which shares the IRA's goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland.

Ahern, facing the prospect of a tiny parliamentary majority or reliance on the backing of Independents to form a government has ruled out seeking electoral support from Sinn Fein's Caoimhghin O Caolain, who won a seat in the Irish parliament.
Asked if he would be in contact with O Caolain, Ahern said it was unlikely and he would probably speak to Adams instead.
Ahern said the Northern Ireland conflict, which has killed 3,200, was a top priority for the next government, and he expected to lead it.

"I think I will almost certainly be Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Ahern said, as counting continued for the last handful of parliament's 166 seats. Both Ahern and Bruton said they would not strike any deal with Sinn Fein until the IRA restores its truce, the condition Britain and Ireland have laid for Sinn Fein's entry into Northern Ireland peace talks in Belfast.
Ahern, who was highly critical of Bruton's handling of a Northern Ireland peace process, said prospects for forging a settlement to the 28-year conflict over the province were "tremendous."
"The possibilities of moving forward are tremendous," he said, referring to the election of a strong Labour government in London.
Mo Mowlam, Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary, has moved swiftly to give the Belfast talks fresh momentum after a year in which they have been bogged in procedural wrangling.
But she has left open whether or not her officials will have any further contact with Sinn Fein after two attempted IRA bomb attacks in Northern Ireland over the past week.

Sinn Fein says it should be at the talks by virtue of its electoral mandate. Adams and his chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, were elected to Britain's parliament on May 1, though they refuse to take their seats because it would entail allegiance to Britain.
But O Caolain will take his Dublin seat after Sinn Fein ended a boycott of the Irish parliament in 1986. reuter ajh
